  Mission Statement
The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth and opportunity,
  and create a joyous and collaborative environment.
  Land Acknowledgment
We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as Tovangaar, the home
 of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as
  all Indigenous people, past, present, and future, and honor their labor as original caretakers of this
land. We commit to uplifting the Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and
  join us in caring for this land.

General Information
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at
320 West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and at
wwww.montereypark.ca.gov/agendas.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.

Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting,
please email City Hall at mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov or call (626) 307-1359 for reasonable
accommodation at least 8 hours before a meeting. Interpretation requests are not guaranteed and are
dependent on availability. Requester will be notified of availability. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

Pursuant to Government Code § 54954.3(a), the public may address the City Council only on matters
listed on this Agenda. No other public comment will be accepted. Pursuant to Rule 5 of Resolution No.
12226 (adopted February 17, 2021), speakers are limited to a total of five minutes for Public Comment.
If desirable, the Mayor and City Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written
Communication will be accepted up to 3 hours before the meeting by completing an online form
at www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.
 The City Council will recess into Closed Session following public comment and the Open Session
items, if any. Public participation is not allowed during Closed Session.

5.  Public Hearing

  5.A. Consideration and possible action to conduct a public hearing to 1) adopt an urgency
   ordinance to enact a citywide prohibition on data centers; 2) introduce and waive first
  reading of a regular ordinance to enact a citywide prohibition on data centers; and 3)
  introduce and waive first reading of a regular ordinance that would implement
  Measure NDC and become effective the same date as Measure NDC, if adopted by
  voters on June 2, 2026

  It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Opening a public hearing to receive written and testimonial evidence regarding a
  potential citywide prohibition on data centers;
  2. After receiving such evidence, consider:
  a. Adopting an urgency ordinance that would take effect immediately upon
  adoption to enact a citywide prohibition on data centers;
  b. Introducing and waiving first reading of a regular ordinance to enact a
  citywide prohibition on data centers;
  c. Introducing and waving first reading of a regular ordinance that would
  implement Measure NDC and become effective the same date as Measure
  NDC, if adopted by voters on June 2, 2026, in accordance with the Elections
  Code and Measure NDC; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act): This Ordinance is not subject to further review
  under the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.;
  “CEQA”) for the following reasons:

  A. It will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
  environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2)). A prohibition on data centers
  means they cannot be constructed.
  B. There is no possibility that the Proposition may have a significant effect on the
  environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15061(b)(3)). A prohibition on data centers
  means they cannot be constructed.
  C. This Ordinance, by itself, do not constitute a “project” as defined in the CEQA
  Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378).
  D. Additionally, CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2) provides that if a project is proposed
  which has been the subject of a prior certified EIR, and “[i]f the [City] finds that
  pursuant to [14 Cal. Code of Regs.] Section 15162, no new effects could occur or
  new mitigation measures would be required, the agency can approve the activity as
  being within the scope of the project covered by the … EIR, and no new
  environmental document would be required.” The City Council finds that it certified a
  Final Environmental Impact Report (“FEIR”) for the Monterey Park Land Use and
  Urban Design Element (as adopted by Ordinance No. 2198 and approved by voters
  as Measure JJ on November 3, 2020) which was filed as State Clearing House No.
  2001-01-1074. This Proposition will not result in any new environmental impact not
  already considered in the FEIR and no further environmental review is required.

6.  Adjournment

  Minutes
  Monterey Park City Council
  Financing Authority (MPFA)
  Housing Authority (MPHA)
  Geologic Hazard Abatement District (GHAD)
  Successor Agency (SA)
  Special Meeting
  April 20, 2026
The City Council, the Financing Authority (MPFA), the Housing Authority (MPHA), the
Geologic Hazard Abatement District (GHAD), and the Successor Agency (SA) of the
City of Monterey Park held a Special Meeting of the Council in the Council Chamber,
located at 320 West Newmark Avenue in the City of Monterey Park Monday, April 20,
2026, at 7:00 p.m.

The Agenda was amended to reflect the live translation information.

1.  Call to Order
  Mayor Yang called the meeting to order at 7:08 p.m.

2.  Roll Call
  City Clerk Maychelle Yee called the roll:

  Council Members Present: Henry Lo, Vinh Ngo, Jose Sanchez, Thomas Wong,
  Elizabeth Yang
  Council Members Absent: None.

  Also present:
  City Manager Inez Alvarez
  City Attorney Karl Berger
  Assistant City Manager Diana Garcia
  Director of Finance Martha Garcia
  Director of Human Resources and Risk Management Christine Tomikawa
  Director of Community Development Timothy Hou
  City Librarian Kristin Olivarez
  Director of Public Works Shawn Igoe
  Police Chief Scott Wiese
  Fire Chief Jason Hing
  Recreation and Community Services Manager Christina Alatorre
  Principal Management Analyst Rebecca Bojorquez
  Deputy City Clerk Cindy Trang

  Virtually present:
  None.

  Mission Statement
The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster growth
and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment
   74-179
  April 20, 2026

3.  Public Communications

4.  Telecommunications Announcement, if requested

5.  Public Hearing

  5.A. Consideration and possible action to conduct a public hearing to 1)
  adopt an urgency ordinance to enact a citywide prohibition on data
  centers; 2) introduce and waive first reading of a regular ordinance to
  enact a citywide prohibition on data centers; and 3) introduce and waive
  first reading of a regular ordinance that would implement Measure NDC
  and become effective the same date as Measure NDC, if adopted by
  voters on June 2, 2026
  The City Council has considered regulating data centers since 2024. Since
  that time, the Council has made various policy choices including amending the
  Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) to regulate data centers in Saturn
  Park; adopting interim moratoria on processing data center applications; and,
  most recently, placing a city-sponsored ballot measure onto the June 2, 2026
  special election (designated as Measure NDC).

  On March 4, 2026, the City Council directed the City Manager and City
  Attorney to initiate a process to consider a citywide prohibition on data centers
  before the voters consider Measure NDC. A public hearing was noticed for a
  special meeting on April 20, 2026, to consider proposed amendments to the
  MPMC prohibiting data centers citywide. If adopted, the three draft ordinances
  would make the same changes to the MPMC: converting the City Council’s
  recent interim actions into a permanent land use policy by prohibiting data
  centers citywide, declaring them a public nuisance, and removing them from
  Saturn Park zoning regulations and the Market Place Specific Plan. They
  would also make it apparent that server rooms are an accessory use to
  otherwise lawful primary land uses.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act): This Ordinance is not subject to
  further review under the California Environmental Quality Act (Public
  Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.; “CEQA”) for the following reasons:

  A. It will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical
  change in the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2)). A
  prohibition on data centers means they cannot be constructed.
  B. There is no possibility that the Proposition may have a significant effect
  on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15061(b)(3)). A prohibition
  on data centers means they cannot be constructed.
  C. This Ordinance, by itself, do not constitute a “project” as defined in the
  CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378).
   74-180
  April 20, 2026

  D. Additionally, CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2) provides that if a project is
  proposed which has been the subject of a prior certified EIR, and “[i]f
  the [City] finds that pursuant to [14 Cal. Code of Regs.] Section 15162,
  no new effects could occur or new mitigation measures would be
  required, the agency can approve the activity as being within the scope
  of the project covered by the … EIR, and no new environmental
  document would be required.” The City Council finds that it certified a
  Final Environmental Impact Report (“FEIR”) for the Monterey Park Land
  Use and Urban Design Element (as adopted by Ordinance No. 2198
  and approved by voters as Measure JJ on November 3, 2020) which
  was filed as State Clearing House No. 2001-01-1074. This Proposition
  will not result in any new environmental impact not already considered
  in the FEIR and no further environmental review is required.

Recommendations:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Opening a public hearing to receive written and testimonial evidence
  regarding a potential citywide prohibition on data centers;
  2. After receiving such evidence, consider:
  a. Adopting an urgency ordinance that would take effect
  immediately upon adoption to enact a citywide prohibition on
  data centers;
  b. Introducing and waiving first reading of a regular ordinance to
  enact a citywide prohibition on data centers;
  c. Introducing and waving first reading of a regular ordinance that
  would implement Measure NDC and become effective the same
  date as Measure NDC, if adopted by voters on June 2, 2026, in
  accordance with the Elections Code and Measure NDC; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

Public Speakers:

  • David Moore, representing the Laborers International Union of North
  America, showed his support of responsible data center development
  jobs. He believed the development of a data center would provide tax
  revenue that supports public services and claimed rejecting projects
  before they are heard from the City Council was unfair.

  • Ralph Velador, on behalf of the Southern California District Council of
  Laborers, stated projects should go through a vetting process and not
  be outlawed before they are heard for consideration.
   74-181
  April 20, 2026

• Dave Jones voiced his support for an ordinance to prohibit data centers
  city-wide and stated that other development opportunities would
  provide long-lasting jobs.

• Felicia Sandoval showed her support for a ban on data centers as she
  believed data centers would not provide anything beneficial for the
  community.

• Yun Wang urged residents to vote 'YES' on Measure NDC, provided
  context on the canvasing efforts from community members, and
  claimed most residents did not want a data center in Monterey Park.

• LS Szeto commented on the residents' desire not to develop a data
  center in the City and instead, develop a project that will benefit the
  community.

• Carrie urged the City Council to vote ‘YES’ on the proposed ordinances
  as she believed the public testimony received in previous City Council
  meetings was enough to decide what is right for Monterey Park.

• Madeline Ocampo showed her support for all three proposed
  ordinances and elaborated on the potential negative effects of data
  centers.

• Emily Chu expressed her support for Agenda Item No. 5.A. and shared
  her appreciation with the City Council for listening to the community.
  She provided context about the negative effects of data centers and
  claimed the residents received a serious breach of trust by the City
  Council.

• Hrag Balian articulated the potential negative effects of data centers in
  a community and urged the City Council to pass the proposed
  ordinances for consideration.

• Larry Bustos, member of the Laborers Union, strongly and respectfully
  opposed the proposed Citywide prohibition of data centers. He believed
  progress and construction meant good local union jobs that provide
  family wages, healthcare and retirement security.

• Jose Radillo spoke in opposition to the proposed ordinance to ban data
  centers permanently. He stated it provides career pathways and allows
  working families to support themselves with dignity.
   74-182
  April 20, 2026

• Vicente Ocampo questioned the union's leadership and clarified that
  the residents’ welcome unions, but not for the development of data
  centers.

• Joyce Vega urged the City Council to pass the proposed ordinances to
  permanently ban data centers and claimed artificial intelligence was not
  a necessity in comparison to clean water and clean air.

• Sam K spoke hoping the City Council would continue to do the right
  thing and permanently ban data centers.

• Cesar Lamas, member of the Laborers International Union of North
  America, spoke about the importance of working to put food on the
  table.

• Chris Lai exhibited a video showcasing the alleged sound data centers
  produce and explained the potential pollution and water consumption a
  data center can bring to the community. He claimed property value
  would decrease and suggested the construction of Whole Foods or
  Trader Joe's.

• Eleanor showed her support for the proposed ordinances and
  requested the City Council to research more on the battery-centered
  storage system as she believed it is a potential fire hazard.

• An unidentifiable registered speaker commented on the resident’s
  decision to not implement a data center and claimed the City is not
  listening to the needs of the residents. She questioned who the City
  Council works for and requested the addition of affordable housing.

• Susan Garcia submitted a speaker card but was not present when her
  name was called.

• Steven Kung, a union member of the Directors Guild and Writers Guild,
  claimed the union members present at the meeting are special interests
  in the pockets of big technological corporations. He reiterated the
  residents' opposition to the development of data centers and
  showcased their support for unions. He elaborated on potential projects
  that provide better revenue and community solidarity.

• Humaira, Pasadena resident, showed her support for the proposed
  ordinance to ban data centers citywide as she believed the
  implementation of one would have negative impacts on the surrounding
  cities.
   74-183
  April 20, 2026

• Jayson Baiz from the Laborers International Union of North America
  spoke in opposition to the proposed ordinances. He claimed the project
  would provide a living wage for their families and taking it away would
  be detrimental to their lives.

• Paul Lange talked about the pros and cons of having job opportunities
  in a community. He provided his input on the amount of passion the
  residents have exhibited throughout the entire process.

• Alice Li expressed her support towards the three proposed ordinances
  and believed they were a crucial step to protecting families and
  children.

• Felicia Marquez articulated her gratitude to the residents who spent
  time fighting for the issue.

• Teresa encouraged the community members to vote 'yes' on Measure
  NDC and emphasized the City Council's need to act on what they
  believe in.

• Angelica thanked the City Council for the time given to the residents for
  public comment. She elaborated on her confusion regarding the Union
  members' claims about the job opportunities a development of a data
  center would bring for the residents.

• Christal Lee provided her input on the proposed ordinances and
  requested the residents to vote 'yes' on Measure NDC.

• Caleb shared his appreciation with the City Council for listening to the
  residents and taking the steps necessary to protect the residents. He
  requested the City Council to include the banning of battery energy
  storage systems as they may potentially lead to uncontrollable
  chemical fires.

• Patrick Chavira echoed Caleb's sentiments regarding the ban of battery
  energy storage systems, and the inclusion of the ban of any large
  operating systems that house illegal data. He claimed the philosophy of
  artificial intelligence is at the expense of others and will replace the
  workforce.

• Al Sanchez submitted a speaker card but was not present when his
  name was called.
   74-184
  April 20, 2026

  • Juan Serrato submitted a speaker card but was not present when his
  name was called.

  • Hosin Mary questioned whether the developer would attempt to reapply
  depending on the outcome results of Measure NDC and expressed her
  research on the recent findings regarding developments of data
  centers.

  • Katherine Guevarra expressed her concerns about the information
  provided by the developers regarding the potential project.

  • Sam Brown shared the importance of protecting working class
  neighborhoods from bearing the costs of massive energy and water
  consumption that only benefits billionaire companies and shared his
  appreciation to the City Council for allowing the speaking time to be 5
  minutes in comparison to neighboring cities.

Discussion: Director of Community Development Hou shared a PowerPoint
presentation detailing the background and timeline leading to the proposed
ordinances, alongside the recommended amendments to the three proposed
ordinances.

The City Council ensued in a discussion regarding the proposed ordinances
and directed staff to research and return to City Council about battery energy
storage systems.

Action Taken: The City Council opened the Public Hearing at 7:08 p.m.,
received written and testimonial evidence regarding a potential citywide
prohibition on data centers, closed the Public Hearing at 8:48 p.m. and
approved the recommendations, as amended to incorporate amendment to
Section 7 of each ordinance by adding the language "Table 21.12(A) in the
MPMC is amended to remove reference to data processing facility.” and
incorporate amendment to Section 8 of each ordinance to reflect title change
of MPMC § 21.14.060 to MPMC § 21.14.055.

Motion: Moved by Council Member Ngo and seconded by Council Member
Sanchez, motion carried by the following vote:

Ayes: Council Members: Henry Lo, Vinh Ngo, Jose Sanchez, Thomas Wong,
Elizabeth Yang
Noes: Council Members: None
Absent: Council Members: None
Abstain: Council Members: None
Recusal: Council Members: None
   74-185
  April 20, 2026

  Urgency Ordinance No. 2276
  An Urgency Ordinance adopting a citywide prohibition on data centers and
  amending the Monterey Park Municipal Code to implement such prohibition

  Ordinance, 1st reading
  An Ordinance adopting a citywide prohibition on data centers and amending
  the Monterey Park Municipal Code to implement such prohibition

  Ordinance, 1st reading
  An Ordinance adopting implementing Measure NDC by establishing a citywide
  prohibition on data centers and amending the Monterey Park municipal code
  to implement such prohibition

6.  Adjournment
  There being no further business for consideration, the meeting was adjourned at
  9:02 p.m.

  _____________________
  Maychelle Yee
  City Clerk
  Approved on July 1, 2026, at the regular City Council Meeting
